checkpoints: The single question that decides the whole topology is WHO asks the registry — everything else follows from that.

Client-side discovery has the consumer query the registry directly (a Consul health endpoint, in this lesson's case) and load-balance the result itself (round-robin, least-connection, whatever the app wants), buying full control over load-balancing logic inside the app — this is also what SDK/HTTP querying against a health endpoint gives you: passing-only filtering and near-real-time blocking queries.
The cost of client-side discovery: each language has to bind its own SDK/client, so a polyglot fleet ends up maintaining N separate client integrations instead of just one.

Server-side discovery flips it: the consumer calls one stable address — a load balancer, a platform Service (Kubernetes ClusterIP + CoreDNS), or a mesh sidecar — and that component queries the registry and forwards the request, so the app never talks to the registry directly and behaves identically no matter what language wrote it.
The cost of server-side discovery: an extra proxy hop the platform must scale and keep healthy.

DNS-based discovery is a third, equally language-agnostic option — any runtime that can resolve a name can discover with zero client dependency — but it is capped by DNS TTL caching (a resolver can keep returning a dead or stale address until the TTL expires) and can't push change events the way a blocking SDK query can.

Recommendation for Team B (polyglot, growing): go server-side — one stable address via a platform Service or mesh sidecar — precisely because it removes the N-client-SDK maintenance burden and decouples every service from ever needing to know Consul exists.

Recommendation for Team A (mono-language, one Go client end to end): can reasonably stay client-side, since there's only one SDK to maintain and, if they want custom LB logic (weighted routing, zone-affinity) baked directly into the app, client-side gives them that control directly instead of pushing it into a proxy's config.
A counter only increases and resets to 0 on restart, so its raw value carries no rate information — you always read it through a per-second rate, never raw.

The flapping here is a query-choice bug: an instantaneous rate over just the last two samples (the `irate()`-style form) is highly reactive and spikes on any transient burst, so an alert built on it false-pages during otherwise normal traffic.
An averaged rate over the whole window (the `rate()`-style form) smooths those spikes out and also compensates for counter resets — exactly what you want for alerting and SLOs.
The fix: build the alert on the windowed rate.
Reserve the instantaneous form for eyeballing short-lived spikes on a dashboard, never for paging.

Both services running the OpenTelemetry SDK with correct startup ordering does not guarantee one continuous trace, because instrumentation only patches the specific modules listed in the SDK's `instrumentations` array — a hand-rolled HTTP client outside that list is invisible to it.

Within a single process, trace context flows automatically through the active context, which is why `tracer.startActiveSpan` correctly nests a new span as a child of the inbound request's span without any manual wiring.

Across a network hop between two services, context has no automatic carrier — it must be transmitted explicitly via the `traceparent` header defined by the W3C Trace Context standard, or the receiving service has no way to know a parent trace exists.

A raw `fetch()` call bypasses Node auto-instrumentation entirely unless a matching instrumentation package (such as `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-undici`) is registered in the SDK's `instrumentations` array, so the outbound request leaves with no `traceparent` header attached.

When a downstream service receives a request carrying no `traceparent` header, its SDK cannot extract any parent context and instead starts a brand-new trace with a fresh `traceId`, which is exactly why Jaeger shows two disconnected traces instead of one parent/child tree.

The break happens specifically at the outbound hop, not at either service's own inbound handling — each service being independently 'instrumented' only covers its own inbound requests, not the manually constructed calls it makes to other services.

The fix is either to route the outbound call through an HTTP client that instrumentation already wraps so the header is injected automatically, or, if the client can't be swapped, to manually call `propagation.inject(context.active(), headers)` from `@opentelemetry/api` before the request is sent.

Confirming the fix means re-running the flow and checking Jaeger for a single shared `traceId` across both services, forming one parent/child tree with the downstream hop's duration visible as a nested span on the timeline instead of hiding inside an orphan trace.

Recording metrics synchronously inside the middleware body, before `next()` is called, means the measurement runs before the handler and `ValidationPipe` ever execute — so the values being recorded do not yet reflect what actually happened to the request.

Hardcoding `status_code: "200"` at that point is wrong because the real status only exists on `res` after the handler (or a `ValidationPipe` rejection) has run; a request rejected with a `400` is therefore mislabeled and counted as a successful `200`.

Computing `durationSec` as the gap between two `process.hrtime.bigint()` calls taken microseconds apart at the top of the middleware measures almost nothing — it captures the time to enter the middleware, not the time the handler and validation actually took to process the request.

This class of bug is dangerous precisely because `httpRequestsTotal.inc()` and `httpRequestDurationSeconds.observe()` never throw or fail — they silently record the wrong labels, so an error-rate dashboard filtering non-2xx status codes stays flat at zero and p95 latency looks impossibly fast even while the service is actually rejecting requests.

The fix is to move the metric recording out of the middleware's synchronous body and into a listener on the `res.on("finish")` event, which only fires after the handler and every middleware/pipe in between — including `ValidationPipe` — has finished and the response has actually been sent.

Inside the `finish` listener, `res.statusCode` holds the true status code (including a `400` from validation) and the duration should be computed from the original `start` timestamp to that moment, so both the counter and the histogram capture what genuinely happened during the request.

`next()` should still be called immediately as before so the request isn't blocked — only the point where the metrics are measured moves to `finish`, not the point where the next middleware in the chain is invoked.

Verifying the fix means sending a request known to fail validation (for example a `400`) and confirming that `/metrics` now shows a `status_code="400"` series on the counter, plus confirming that latency observations for successful requests reflect the handler's real processing time instead of clustering near zero.

Logging and error tracking are two separate observability pillars: a call like `logger.error(...)` only appends a line to the central log store, while a grouped issue, captured stack trace, and frequency-based alert are produced by the error-tracking pillar (e.g. Sentry) and only happen when that pillar actually receives the exception.
A `catch` block that logs a failure and returns a fallback value (such as `null`) without rethrowing stops the exception right there — it never propagates further up the call stack.

A framework-level global exception filter (e.g. `SentryGlobalFilter` registered via `APP_FILTER`) only runs for exceptions that propagate up through the request pipeline; if a `catch` block swallows the error and returns normally, the handler looks like a success from the framework's point of view, so the filter never executes and the error tracker never records anything.
Swallowing an exception is not inherently a bug — returning a fallback for a genuinely optional side effect can be the correct design.

The defect in code like this is that a real production incident (e.g. a payment refund silently failing) gets hidden behind a log line and a response that looks successful, with no mechanism to surface that it is happening at scale.
One valid fix is to remove the local `catch` (or rethrow a typed exception from it) so the error propagates naturally into the global exception filter, which then reports it to the tracker.

If returning a fallback truly is the correct behavior for that code path, the alternative fix is to keep the `catch` but explicitly call the error tracker's capture method (e.g. `Sentry.captureException(err)`) inside it before returning the fallback, so the failure is still recorded even though it never reaches the global filter.

Correctness of the fix should be verified by deliberately forcing the failing call to throw and confirming that a grouped issue with a full stack trace appears in the error tracker — not just by checking that a line was written to the log store.
A secret manager is not "a safer `.env` file" — its real value is separating the secret from the artifact and fetching it at runtime over an authenticated API, instead of being baked in statically.
To authenticate to Vault in the first place, the app still holds one bootstrap credential — the secret-zero — and here that is a token sitting in env.
Vault does not eliminate that bootstrap problem, it just MOVES the trust: instead of the DB password living in env, now a Vault token lives in env, while the real DB password lives only inside Vault.
The win is still real: the blast radius collapses from scattered `.env` files, image layers, and CI variables down to exactly one place (Vault).
Rotating the real password becomes changing a single entry rather than rebuilding and redeploying the artifact.

In a mature production setup, that leftover credential — the token in env — gets shrunk one step further into an identity issued directly by the platform: a Kubernetes service-account JWT, or a cloud IAM role, so no human-readable secret ever sits on disk longer than a few minutes.
One-way TLS (as on a public HTTPS website) only has the client verify the server; that's sufficient for the public web because the server doesn't need to know "who" is calling at the TLS layer.
Mutual TLS adds the reverse direction: the server also requires and verifies the client's certificate, with both sides vouched for by one shared CA.

"The caller is inside our VPC/cluster" is not an authentication model because a compromised node (RCE, malicious dependency, misconfigured pod) sits inside the network by default and can move laterally to call every internal service freely — the system trusts anyone with an internal IP.
Zero-trust flips that default: every request must prove its own identity with a certificate.
That identity comes from the CA-signed cert's CN/SAN, never a self-declared header — a header is forgeable, a cert is not (short of the CA's private key leaking).

The switch that turns on two-way verification lives on the SERVER side: the server must actively request and verify the client's cert (e.g. requestCert+rejectUnauthorized, client-auth=need, RequireAndVerifyClientCert).

Without that server-side switch, the client cert is merely optional — the server still accepts a connection even when no client cert is presented, and the zero-trust model collapses right at authentication.

A WAF middleware that inspects only `req.body` leaves the query string, the path, cookies, and headers open — headers such as `X-Forwarded-For` and `Referer` are classic places attackers stash SQLi/XSS payloads precisely because teams often check only the body.
Coverage limited to a single input surface makes a WAF a false sense of security rather than real protection, even when the team believes the API is already "protected."

Echoing the offending payload back inside a 403 response — e.g. `res.status(403).json({ status: 'blocked', input: req.body })` — turns the very control meant to stop injection into a reflected-XSS sink.
A block response should carry only `{ status, rule }` and never a copy of the input that was submitted, since the response itself becomes an attack vector otherwise.

Wiring the middleware with `consumer.apply(WafMiddleware).forRoutes(OrdersController)` instead of `forRoutes('*')` leaves every other controller in the app with zero WAF coverage, not partial coverage.

With no cap on request body size, a very large payload makes the inspection scan run against the entire body, turning the WAF's own inspection step into a CPU/DoS amplifier — the opposite of what a security control is meant to do.

The reflection sink is the highest-priority fix because it's an active vulnerability today, not just a gap; the input-surface gap and the route-coverage gap can be closed together next since both already let attackers sail through untouched; a body-size cap comes last as hardening.

Even a fully-fixed WAF remains a backstop, not a replacement for parameterized queries and output encoding — treating it as the whole defense leaves a team over-trusting a filter that a well-encoded attack can still slip past.
Unwrapping a DEK means sending the wrapped key to a KMS like Vault Transit and getting the plaintext key back over HTTP — each unwrap is a full network round-trip, not a local operation.

Calling `TransitService.unwrapDek` on every single read means the same record's DEK gets re-unwrapped from Vault on every request, even when it was just decrypted moments earlier, so the KMS round-trip dominates read latency.

Looping over N rows and `await`-ing `unwrapDek` inside the loop sequentially turns a batch/list endpoint into an N+1 pattern against the KMS: N records cost N separate HTTP round-trips whose latencies stack up one after another.

Putting the KMS directly on the hot read path also makes it a single point of failure for reads — if Vault slows down or becomes unreachable, every read request fails along with it, not just the writes that actually need fresh key material.

Caching the unwrapped DEK in memory for a short TTL (for example a `Map` keyed by wrapped DEK or record id storing `{ dek, expiresAt }`) lets repeat reads of the same record skip the Vault round-trip entirely until the entry expires.

The DEK cache must live only in process memory and never be written to disk, so a crash or restart loses it exactly as if it had never been cached — this preserves envelope-encryption's bounded blast radius and crypto-shredding guarantees, since the plaintext key never becomes durable outside Vault.

Fixing the N+1 in the batch endpoint means collecting all the wrapped DEKs and sending them in a single request to Vault Transit's batch endpoint (using a `batch_input` array) instead of issuing one `unwrapDek` call per row — this collapses N round-trips into one.

Running Vault Transit in high availability, such as multiple nodes behind a load balancer or Enterprise performance replicas, removes the single-node-failure risk so one Vault instance going down doesn't take every read with it, and the fix should be validated by comparing round-trip counts and p50/p99 read latency before and after, plus a test confirming the DEK cache actually expires at its TTL and is never persisted outside memory.

Calling `repo.find({ order: { index: "ASC" } })` materializes every row of the audit table into memory before the loop even starts, so the endpoint pays a full-table scan on every single request regardless of how many rows were already verified in a prior call.

The verification loop always seeds `expectedPrev` with `GENESIS_PREV_HASH` and re-walks the chain from index 0 on every call, making the cost O(n) in both time and CPU — one hash recomputation per row, every time, no matter how many earlier calls already proved the older entries intact.

A health/monitoring probe hitting this same endpoint every few seconds turns an already-expensive full-scan-plus-full-recompute into continuous, unbounded load on the database as the audit log grows toward tens of millions of rows.

Storing a periodic checkpoint — `{ count, entryHash, anchoredAt }` — written by a background job lets verification start from the last confirmed position instead of genesis, bounding both memory and recompute work to only the rows appended since that checkpoint.

The checkpoint must be mirrored somewhere the application's own database role does not also control — an external notary, a second datastore, or a SIEM — otherwise the checkpoint is exactly as forgeable as the hash chain it is meant to protect.

Streaming rows instead of loading them all with `repo.find()` (e.g., a query-builder `.stream()` returning a Node `Readable`) keeps memory flat regardless of table size; this is a separate fix from checkpointing, which bounds the recompute work rather than the memory footprint.

An internally consistent hash chain cannot detect truncation: if the newest rows are deleted after the last checkpoint, the remaining chain still verifies correctly, so an incremental scan over the surviving tail has nothing to compare against and would wrongly report success.

Catching truncation requires comparing the current tail's count and entryHash against a value anchored externally and independently of the primary datastore — an in-place edit changes a hash, but a deletion of the newest rows just makes the chain shorter, and only an external anchor exposes that difference.

Moving from full re-hash to checkpoint-based incremental verification shifts the trust boundary from the per-row hash to the checkpoint and the witness's independence, so a sparser anchoring cadence widens the window in which an attacker could time an edit and a truncation to land undetected before the next anchor runs.
